subject: history
displayName: KS3 History — The Interwar Period: Dictatorships & Appeasement
subtitle: The rise of Hitler and Mussolini, the failures of appeasement, and the road to World War II.

topics: The Rise of Hitler and the Nazi Party

data.targetWord: A system of government in which one ruler or one party holds almost total power, often using force, propaganda and censorship.

examples.en-GB: Nazi Germany became a dictatorship after Hitler destroyed democratic checks on his power in 1933.

topics: The Rise of Hitler and the Nazi Party

data.targetWord: An extreme nationalist political movement that rejects democracy, supports strong leadership and uses violence against opponents.

examples.en-GB: Mussolini's fascism in Italy shared features with Hitler's Nazism but differed in important ways.

topics: The Rise of Hitler and the Nazi Party

data.targetWord: The ideology of Hitler and the Nazi Party, combining extreme nationalism, dictatorship, racism and antisemitism.

examples.en-GB: Nazism placed racist antisemitism at the centre of state policy in Germany from 1933.

topics: Life in Nazi Germany

data.targetWord: Information, images or messages designed to persuade people to think or behave in a particular way, used extensively by dictatorships.

examples.en-GB: Joseph Goebbels led Nazi propaganda, controlling posters, radio, films and rallies.

topics: Life in Nazi Germany

data.targetWord: The control or banning of information, books, newspapers, films or speeches that the government dislikes.

examples.en-GB: The Nazis burned books they disapproved of and banned opposition newspapers through censorship.

topics: Life in Nazi Germany

data.targetWord: The use of fear, violence, arrest or imprisonment to control a population and suppress opposition.

examples.en-GB: The Gestapo and SS used terror to silence political opponents of the Nazi regime.

topics: The Rise of Hitler and the Nazi Party

data.targetWord: A severe worldwide economic crisis beginning in 1929, causing mass unemployment, business failures and widespread poverty.

examples.en-GB: The Great Depression helped the Nazi Party gain support by making extreme promises attractive to desperate voters.

topics: Appeasement and the Road to War

data.targetWord: A policy of making concessions to an aggressive power in the hope of preserving peace and avoiding conflict.

examples.en-GB: British Prime Minister Chamberlain pursued appeasement by allowing Germany to take the Sudetenland at Munich.

topics: Appeasement and the Road to War

data.targetWord: The union of Germany and Austria in March 1938, carried out by Hitler despite it being forbidden by the Treaty of Versailles.

examples.en-GB: The Anschluss brought Austria under Nazi control and expanded Germany's territory and population.

topics: Appeasement and the Road to War

data.targetWord: The September 1938 agreement between Britain, France, Germany and Italy that allowed Germany to take the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia.

examples.en-GB: Chamberlain returned from Munich claiming the agreement had preserved peace, but Hitler soon broke his promises.

topics: The Rise of Hitler and the Nazi Party

data.targetWord: A law passed in March 1933 that gave Hitler the power to make laws without the German parliament, destroying democratic checks on his authority.

examples.en-GB: The Enabling Act allowed Hitler to create a dictatorship by bypassing the Reichstag.

topics: Life in Nazi Germany

data.targetWord: Antisemitic laws introduced in Nazi Germany in 1935 that stripped Jewish people of citizenship and banned marriage with non-Jewish Germans.

examples.en-GB: The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 made antisemitic discrimination official state policy in Germany.

topics: Life in Nazi Germany

data.targetWord: Prejudice, hostility or discrimination against Jewish people, made central to Nazi state ideology.

examples.en-GB: Nazi antisemitism grew from early boycotts and propaganda into state-sponsored violence and law.

topics: The Rise of Hitler and the Nazi Party

data.targetWord: The democratic government of Germany from 1919 until Hitler destroyed it in 1933, named after the city where its constitution was written.

examples.en-GB: The Weimar Republic struggled with economic crises and political instability that helped extremists gain support.

topics: The Rise of Hitler and the Nazi Party

data.targetWord: The collapse of share prices in the United States in October 1929 that triggered the global Great Depression.

examples.en-GB: The Wall Street Crash of 1929 caused German unemployment to rise sharply, strengthening extremist parties.

topics: Life in Nazi Germany

data.targetWord: A Nazi organisation for young people that aimed to instil loyalty to Hitler, discipline and Nazi beliefs.

examples.en-GB: The Hitler Youth trained boys in military discipline and loyalty to the Nazi regime.

topics: Appeasement and the Road to War

data.targetWord: The rebuilding of armed forces and weapons, particularly Germany's illegal expansion of its military in the 1930s.

examples.en-GB: Hitler announced German rearmament in 1935, openly breaking the Treaty of Versailles.

topics: Appeasement and the Road to War

data.targetWord: An international organisation created after 1918 to keep peace through collective security, but weakened by absent members and lack of enforcement powers.

examples.en-GB: The League of Nations failed to stop Japan in Manchuria and Italy in Abyssinia in the 1930s.

topics: Appeasement and the Road to War

data.targetWord: A border region of Czechoslovakia with a large German-speaking population, demanded by Hitler and given to Germany at the Munich Agreement in 1938.

examples.en-GB: The Sudetenland was handed to Germany at Munich, weakening Czechoslovakia's defences.

topics: Life in Nazi Germany

data.targetWord: The Nazi secret state police, which used surveillance, torture and arrest to suppress opposition to the regime.

examples.en-GB: The Gestapo created fear by monitoring citizens and arresting those suspected of opposing the Nazis.

topics: Life in Nazi Germany

data.targetWord: A violent organised attack on Jewish homes, businesses and synagogues across Germany and Austria on 9-10 November 1938, also called Kristallnacht.

examples.en-GB: The November Pogrom of 1938 showed that Nazi persecution had moved from discrimination to open organised violence.

topics: The Rise of Hitler and the Nazi Party

data.targetWord: The payments Germany was forced to make to the Allies under the Treaty of Versailles as compensation for wartime damage.

examples.en-GB: German resentment over reparations gave Hitler powerful propaganda material against the Weimar Republic.

topics: Appeasement and the Road to War

data.targetWord: A non-aggression agreement signed between Germany and the Soviet Union in August 1939, secretly dividing parts of eastern Europe between them.

examples.en-GB: The Nazi-Soviet Pact freed Germany to invade Poland without fear of Soviet interference.

topics: Life in Nazi Germany

data.targetWord: Describing a dictatorship that seeks to control most aspects of public and private life, including politics, culture, media and education.

examples.en-GB: Nazi Germany is often described as a totalitarian state because it controlled information, culture and youth organisations.

topics: Appeasement and the Road to War

data.targetWord: The principle that countries should work together through an international organisation to prevent aggression and protect peace.

examples.en-GB: The League of Nations was based on collective security, but lacked the power to enforce it effectively.

data.title: Key events on the road to war — put in chronological order
items: Wall Street Crash and start of the Great Depression (1929)
Nuremberg Laws strip Jewish people of citizenship (1935)
Munich Agreement — Germany takes the Sudetenland (September 1938)
Germany invades Poland — Second World War begins (1 September 1939)

topics: The Rise of Hitler and the Nazi Party

data.title: Hitler's steps to power — put these in the correct order
items: Wall Street Crash increases unemployment in Germany (1929)
Nazis become the largest party in elections but without a majority (1932)
Hitler appointed Chancellor by conservative politicians (January 1933)
Enabling Act gives Hitler power to rule by decree (March 1933)
Nazi dictatorship consolidated with ban on other parties

topics: Life in Nazi Germany

data.title: Stages of Nazi persecution before the Holocaust — put in order
items: Boycott of Jewish shops and job restrictions (1933)
Nuremberg Laws remove Jewish citizenship rights (1935)
November Pogrom — organised violence against Jewish communities (November 1938)
Ghettos established in occupied Poland (1939 onwards)
